If your car’s engine isn’t performing up to par or the “Check Engine” light goes on, have it inspected immediately. Failure to do so can reduce your mileage per gallon of fuel or cause your vehicle to pollute. | Engine Cooling System | The engine cooling system affects your car’s overall dependability and engine longevity. Cooling systems have advanced over the years with new coolant formulations and new radiator designs and materials. If you suspect a problem with your cooling system, you should check it immediately. | Engine Replacement | When a car or truck suffers major engine damage, the first reaction of most vehicle owners is to buy a new or used car or truck. This makes sense in some cases, but often, it isn’t necessary. Repowering your car or truck’s worn out engine with a rebuilt/remanufactured engine can also be considerably less expensive than buying a new or used car. | Exhaust and Mufflers | Your car’s exhaust system has come a long way from the old days of exhaust pipes and mufflers. Today, the exhaust system is safety and emissions control rolled into one. Have your car’s exhaust system inspected regularly and check it immediately if you suspect any problems. | Steering and Suspension | Like your car’s brake system, the steering and suspension systems are key safety-related systems. Together, they largely determine your car’s ride and handling. Have your car’s steering and suspension systems checked regularly, at least once a year and usually with a wheel alignment. | Timing Belt | In a piston engine, either a timing belt or timing chain or set of timing gears is used to synchronize the rotation of the crankshaft and the camshaft. This synchronisation ensures that the engine's valves open and close at the correct times in relation to the position of the pistons. A worn timing belt will affect your engine's starting speed as it is attached to the pulleys that drive the crankshaft. Eventually, the belt can slip on the camshaft drive causing the engine cylinder to open and close at the wrong time. | Transmission | You car’s belts and hoses are essential to the cooling, air conditioning and charging systems, and the engine. Don’t take these routine replacement intervals for granted because they can break down and leave you stranded. | Request an Appointment | Maintenance | About our Maintenance services | Belts and Hoses | Many experts urge replacing belts, radiator and heater hoses at specific recommended intervals to prevent your car from breaking down. Losing a belt today can mean big trouble for the engine because serpentine belts are used on most engines to turn the water pump, alternator, power steering and air-conditioning compressor. If the belt snaps, everything is lost and you may be stranded. Older cars use individual V-belts for these various accessories. A blown hose could result in an overheated engine and can cause additional engine damage. | Cabin Air Filter | A filter used to clean incoming air for the car’s HVAC system. Introduced in European vehicles, cabin air filters are now becoming common on more domestic and Asian makes and models. Some examples include the Ford Taurus, Contour, Windstar and Ford trucks; the Chevrolet Impala, Monte Carlo, Suburban, Tahoe and Silverado; and the Lincoln Navigator. Japanese cars such as the Honda Accord and Odyssey, and the Acura RL and TL use cabin filters. To date, approximately 40% of cars have cabin air filters, but the number grows each year. | Fuel Economy | Fuel economy is the number of miles/kilometers per gallon your car gets and this can vary depending on how you maintain and drive your vehicle. Low tire pressure, a clogged air filter, worn or fouled spark plugs can lower gas mileage – as much as 33 percent on the highway and five percent on city streets – as does excessive idling, driving over the speed limit and using the car’s A/C system. | Fuel Filter | The typical fuel filter for most fuel-injected cars consists of a high-pressure canister filled with filtering media. Filters may have clamped, threaded or special fittings to ensure reliable connection to the fuel system. Filters for carbureted engines may be located at the inlet of the carburetor or inline. Start by checking the tire pressure regularly—especially during colder months when air pressure fluctuates. Catching signs of trouble early can help prevent a minor issue from turning into a full-blown breakdown. But how can you tell if your transmission is starting to act up? Here’s a closer look at the early warning signs and what you can do to keep your car running smoothly. | ‍ | Unusual Sounds When Shifting Gears | One of the first signs of trouble is strange noises when shifting gears. If you notice a grinding or clunking sound as you change gears, it may be time to check out the transmission. These sounds often indicate worn parts or a lack of transmission fluid, which helps keep it lubricated and functioning smoothly. | Pay attention to: | Grinding noises : Common in manual transmissions but can also happen in automatics. | Clunking sounds : Can indicate a worn transmission or failing internal components. | Catching these sounds early on can save you from more expensive repairs down the road. | ‍ | Delayed Shifts or Slipping Gears | If your car hesitates or “slips” when shifting gears, it’s often a sign of transmission issues. Delayed shifting means it isn’t engaging as quickly as it should, while slipping gears can cause the car to unexpectedly switch out of gear. Both problems can be dangerous, especially if they happen on the highway or in heavy traffic. | Signs of delayed shifts or slipping include: | Hesitation when accelerating from a stop. | The engine revving without gaining speed . | Unexpected drops in speed when driving normally. | If you experience any of these symptoms, consider having your transmission checked before it potentially gets worse. | ‍ | MORE > | ID Minor Vehicle Issues Before They Become BIG Problems | ‍ | Fluid Leaks Under the Vehicle | Transmission fluid is crucial for keeping it lubricated and preventing overheating. Leaks can lead to low fluid levels, which can cause the transmission to wear out faster. If you notice a reddish or dark brown puddle under your car, it’s likely transmission fluid and a signal to have your vehicle inspected. | It’s essential to: | Check for fluid regularly if you’ve had a previous leak. | Get leaks repaired promptly to prevent additional damage. | Even a small leak can lead to significant transmission damage if left unchecked. | ‍ | ‍ | Burning Smell While Driving | A burning odor while driving is always a reason for concern, especially if it’s coming from the transmission. | This smell is often due to overheating or low fluid levels, both of which can damage the internal components. If you catch a burning smell, don’t ignore it—this could mean your transmission is in need of immediate attention. | Causes of a burning smell include: | Low transmission fluid levels . | Excessive friction in the transmission. | Overheating due to clogged filters or other issues. | Taking your car in at the first sign of a burning smell can save you from more extensive repairs. | ‍ | Difficulty Changing Gears | If you find that shifting gears has become difficult or feels rough, this can signal big trouble. Whether it’s a manual or automatic transmission, problems with shifting are often linked to worn or damaged components, low transmission fluid, or failing sensors. | Signs to watch for: | Hard shifts that require extra force. | Inconsistent gear changes or “jerky” movements. | Unresponsive gears when you try to shift. | When shifting becomes difficult, it’s best to address the issue quickly to avoid being stranded due to a failing transmission. | ‍ | Need Help with Transmission Issues? | Stay cool – noticing these early signs can prevent a minor issue from turning into a costly car repair. Rotating your tires is a quick and simple way to help them last longer and perform better. | ‍ | So, How Often Should You Rotate Your Tires? | Most manufacturers recommend getting your tires rotated every 5,000 to 7,000 miles. That usually lines up with your oil change schedule, so it’s easy to remember and knock out both at the same time. If you’re not sure what your car needs, check your owner’s manual or | ask your mechanic. | ‍ | Some signs you might be overdue for a tire rotation: | Uneven tread wear | Vibrations while driving | Your car pulls to one side | Rotating your tires means moving them from one position to another, like front to back or side to side, to help them wear more evenly. This helps with traction, fuel efficiency, and extends the life of your tires. But if you don't take care of your car, how can it reliably get you from Point A to Point B? If you find yourself avoiding looking at the service sticker or those 'pesky' alert lights, here's how to tell if your car truly needs an oil change ASAP. | Signs Your Car Needs an Oil Change | ‍ | Okay, we've mentioned the dashboard warning lights - if you see that oil pressure light or check engine light flashing, these are your car's built-in signals begging you to | schedule maintenance | . But what are some other clear signs it's time to swing by an oil change shop: | ‍ | Unusual Engine Noise: Are you hearing ticking, tapping, or knocking noises? These sounds may mean your engine is begging for new oil to keep everything running smoothly. | Excessive Exhaust Smoke: If you see more smoke than usual from your tailpipe, it might be time to drain the old oil for a fresh change. | Burnt Oil Smell: A pungent, burnt oil aroma could signal that your engine's oil is past its prime and struggling to lubricate effectively. | Decreased Fuel Efficiency: Paying more frequent visits to the gas station? This might mean your car is thirsty for an oil change to optimize performance. | Oil Appearance: You can pop the hood and take a quick look at the oil stick. Notice dark, dirty, or gritty oil? It's time for an appointment. Fresh oil should be clear with a slight amber hue – not murky or opaque. | Don't let these signs go unchecked! Visit Ice Cold Air today and let our expert technicians give your vehicle the care it deserves. Schedule your oil change now and ask about our FREE visual inspection to ensure smooth and efficient driving. | How Often Should Oil Changes Be Done? | Even if you are not experiencing the signs above, you have to stay on top of car maintenance. It's best to follow the oil change schedule outlined in your owner’s manual, as each | vehicle | is different. Most newer cars can comfortably go between 6,000 to 15,000 miles between oil changes, thanks to advancements in engine technology and oil formulations. | ‍ | However, there are circumstances where you might need to adjust when you should get an oil change: If you frequently drive in stop-and-go traffic, often tow heavy loads, or regularly take short trips (where the engine doesn't fully heat up), your car might benefit from more frequent oil changes. | ‍ | For those with older cars, sticking closer to the traditional recommendation of every 3,000 miles (5K max) is a best practice. Not only does this ensure peak performance, but it also helps in spotting other potential | car maintenance | issues early on! | ‍ | ‍ | Affordable Oil Changes for All Makes & Models | At the end of the day, keeping your vehicle in top shape comes down to paying attention and taking action when needed. Especially with the cost of parts today, you may wonder why it's often recommended to replace your rotors when changing brake pads. Our techs aren't trying to upsell you, you know we'd never take advantage, but we do want to keep your ride smooth & safe. | ‍ | As you know, your car’s braking system is a vital component in vehicle safety. | Brake pads | and rotors work together to bring your car to a stop. The pads press against the rotors to create the friction needed to slow down or halt your vehicle. Over time, both of these parts wear out and need replacement. | ‍ | Why replace rotors with pads, you ask? The main reason is to maintain the integrity of your braking system.
